Kenney 1-Bit Pack

Kenney’s public-domain sheet of more than 1,000 game tiles draws every tree, wall, monster, weapon, icon, and letter on a 16-pixel grid with a few flat colors.

OpenGameArt: 1-Bit Pack

Evidence
Downloaded 1bitpack_kenney_1.1.zip from the OpenGameArt page and inspected Tilesheet/colored_packed.png (768 × 352 px) enlarged 2× to 1536 × 704 px. The file has exactly 8 colors. The sample map on the page was not used, because it is resampled (254 colors) and carries a license banner.

2 October 2026
Rights
Open license, stored. License: CC0-1.0. Rights policy

Context

OpenGameArt describes the pack as more than 1,000 tiles, characters, objects, and items for roguelike and RPG games, with tiles for UI, platformers, and puzzle games, a monochrome version, and transparent versions. OpenGameArt.

The License.txt in the download says “Created/distributed by Kenney (www.kenney.nl)”, “Creation date: 06-05-2020”, and “License: (Creative Commons Zero, CC0)”. The OpenGameArt page shows the submission date 6 May 2019, so the 2020 date is probably version 1.1. OpenGameArt.

Observed

  • A dense grid of 16 × 16 tiles on a dark plum ground (#472d3c).
  • Most tiles are one flat light color (#cfc6b8): characters, skulls, swords, bows, walls, fences, furniture, and frames.
  • A few groups use one accent each: green trees and plants, blue water, brown furniture, red bricks and playing cards, yellow coins and crowns.
  • The sheet has a full bitmap alphabet and digits, arrows, hearts, crosses, dice, and warning signs at the lower right.
  • Shading is absent. Each sprite is a silhouette with interior lines cut out of it.
  • All diagonals, such as the swords and the diamond frame, step one pixel at a time.

Why it belongs

The pack shows the most reduced form of the style: one color per object and one pixel unit for everything. It reads as game art without any shading.

The sheet is also a ready inventory of the game furniture that the rubric names: hearts, coins, keys, cursors, frames, and a pixel alphabet.

Borrow

Draw icons as one-color silhouettes on a 16-pixel grid, and color each family of icons with one accent.

Use a dark, slightly warm ground instead of pure black, so the light pixels read softly.
